Non-Axiomatic Reasoning System (NARS) processes tasks imposed by its environment, which may include human users or other computer systems. Tasks can arrive at any time, and there is no restriction on their contents as far as they can be expressed in __Narsese__, the I/O language of NARS.
* **Question** - To process it means to find the best answer to it according to current beliefs.
As a reasoning system, the architecture of NARS consists of a **memory**, an **inference engine**, and a **control mechanism**.

At the current time, the most comprehensive description of NARS are the books Rigid Flexibility: The Logic of Intelligence and Non-Axiomatic Logic: A Model of Intelligent Reasoning . Various aspects of the system are introduced and discussed in many papers, most of which are available here.

**Jinbase** (pronounced as **/ˈdʒɪnˌbeɪs/**) is a multi-model transactional embedded database that uses SQLite as storage engine. Its reference implementation is an eponymous lightweight Python library available on PyPI.

Having SQLite as the storage engine allows Jinbase to benefit from transactions. Jinbase ensures that at the top level, reads and writes on key-value, depot, queue and stack stores are transactional. For user convenience, context managers are exposed to create transactions of different modes.

When for a write operation, the user submits data, whether it is a dictionary, string or integer, Jinbase serializes (except binary data), chunks and stores the data iteratively with the Paradict compact binary data format. This then allows for the smooth storage of complex data of arbitrary size with Jinbase.

SQLite has an impressive capability which is incremental I/O for BLOBs. While this capability is designed to target an individual BLOB column in a row, Jinbase extends this so that for each record, incremental reads cover all chunks as if they were a single unified BLOB.

For dictionary records only, Jinbase automatically creates and maintains a lightweight index consisting of pointers to root fields, which then allows extracting from an arbitrary record the contents of a field automatically deserialized before being returned.

Jinbase exposes a database connection object to the underlying SQLite storage engine, allowing for sophisticated configuration. The Paradict binary data format used for serializing records also allows for customizing data types via a `paradict.TypeRef` object.

Jinbase implements persistence for familiar data models whose stores coexist in a single file with an intuitive programmatic interface. Supported data types range from simple to complex and of arbitrary size.
The key-value data model associates to a string or an integer key, a value that is serializable with the Paradict binary data format.

String keys can be searched with a glob) pattern and integer keys can be searched within a range of numbers. Since records are automatically timestamped, a `time_range` tuple can be provided by the user to search for them as well as keys.
> Check out the API reference for the key-value store.
The depot data model shares similarities with the List) data structure. An
unique identifier (UID) is automatically assigned to a record appended to the store. This record can be retrieved later either by its unique identifier or by its 0-based position in the store.
> Check out the API reference for the depot store.

The queue) data model like other stores, is transactional. While this store provides methods to enqueue and dequeue records, there is also `peek_xxx` methods to look at the record at the front or the back of the queue, that is, read it without dequeuing.
> Check out the API reference for the queue store.

The stack) data model like other stores, is transactional. While this store provides methods to push and pop records, there is also a `peek` method to look at the record on top of the stack, that is, read it without popping it from the stack.
> Check out the API reference for the stack store.
As Jinbase uses SQLite as its storage engine, it de facto supports the relational data model for which it exposes an interface, LiteDBC, for querying SQLite.

LiteDBC is an SQL interface compliant with the DB-API 2.0 specification described by PEP 249, itself wrapping Python's sqlite3 module for a more intuitive interface and multithreading support by default.

When for a write operation, the user submits data, whether it is a dictionary, string or integer, Jinbase serializes (except binary data), chunks and stores the data iteratively with the Paradict compact binary data format. Under the hood, these chunks are actually stored as SQLite Binary Large Objects (BLOBs).

SQLite has an impressive capability which is incremental I/O for BLOBs. While this capability is designed to target an individual BLOB column in a row, Jinbase extends it to enable incremental reads of record chunks as if they form a single unified BLOB.
